title: 08. Microservices & Architecture Patterns: Configuration Management
summary: Configuration management in microservices is the practice of externalizing environment-specific and runtime-mutable settings (database URLs, feature flags, rate limits, timeouts) from application code into a separate config…
objectives: What is the difference between static and dynamic configuration, and when would you choose each?
How does layered configuration work, and what is the precedence order?
What is hot reload, and how does it actually propagate to the application code?
How do you manage secrets differently from other configuration?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Configuration management in microservices is the practice of externalizing environment-specific and runtime-mutable settings (database URLs, feature flags, rate limits, timeouts) from application code into a separate config layer — static (env vars, files) or dynamic (a central config server with hot reload) — so that the same binary can run unchanged across dev/staging/prod and operators can tune behavior without redeploying.

In a monolith, configuration is often an afterthought — a `config.yaml` next to the binary, or a `properties` file on the classpath, edited once at deploy time. In a microservices system, this approach collapses. There are dozens or hundreds of services, each with its own config, deployed across multiple environments (dev, staging, prod, multiple regions), each with potentially hundreds of settings (DB credentials, downstream URLs, cache TTLs, feature flags, rate limits, circuit-breaker thresholds). Hardcoding any of these in the binary means redeploying to change a value — unacceptable when a rate limit needs to drop from 1000 to 100 req/s during an incident, or when a feature flag needs to flip off across 50 services in seconds. Worse, baking secrets (DB passwords, API keys) into the binary or the image is a security disaster waiting to happen. Configuration management solves this by separating config from code: the binary is generic, the config is external, and the runtime merges them. The Twelve-Factor App methodology (Heroku, 2011) codified this as "Store config in the environment" — though in practice, the environment is just one of several config sources.

Config sources fall on a spectrum from **static** to **dynamic**. **Static config** is fixed at process start: environment variables (set in the container spec or systemd unit), `.env` files, or mounted config files. These are simple, ubiquitous, and have zero runtime overhead — but they require a process restart to change. **Dynamic config** is fetched at runtime from a config server: Spring Cloud Config (a Git-backed HTTP server), HashiCorp Consul KV (a distributed key-value store with watch/notify), AWS Parameter Store / AppConfig, etcd, or ZooKeeper. The service polls or subscribes to the config server, and when a value changes, it receives the update without restart. Dynamic config is more complex (a new distributed dependency, a client library, fallback behavior when the server is down), but it enables hot reload — flipping a feature flag, tuning a circuit breaker, or rotating a secret without redeploying. The standard pattern is **layered config**: a base config file (defaults) is overlaid by environment-specific values (env vars for secrets, config server for tunables), with later layers overriding earlier ones. The service resolves the final value once at startup (static) or continuously (dynamic).

The real-world journey that made dynamic config mainstream was Netflix's Archaius. In 2011–2013, Netflix was migrating from a monolith to hundreds of microservices on AWS, and they needed a way to tune behavior at runtime — circuit-breaker thresholds, rate limits, feature flags, regional failover toggles — without redeploying. Archaius (open-sourced in 2012, now part of the NetflixOSS stack) provided a layered, dynamic configuration library for the JVM: it chained multiple config sources (system properties, environment, files, a remote DB-backed source), polled the remote source every 30 seconds, and fired change events to listeners when a value changed. A Netflix engineer could flip a feature flag in the database and watch it propagate to thousands of instances in 30 seconds, no deploy needed. Airbnb had a parallel journey with **Diamond** (2014, open-sourced): a Python-based config system where services subscribed to a Diamond server (backed by a database), and config changes were pushed via long-poll. Both companies built these because the velocity of operational tuning at scale demanded hot reload — redeploying 1000 instances to change a rate limit was not viable. Spring Cloud Config (2015) brought the same model to the Spring ecosystem: a Git-backed config server that served environment-specific YAML, with clients refreshing via a `/actuator/refresh` endpoint or a Spring Cloud Bus broadcast. Modern systems lean on managed services — AWS Parameter Store (free tier, IAM-integrated), AWS AppConfig (deployment-aware config rollouts with baked-in validation), GCP Secret Manager, Azure App Configuration — which removes the operational burden of running a config server.

The trade-offs of dynamic config are real and often underestimated. **Operational dependency**: the config server becomes a critical dependency — if it is down, services either freeze their last-known config (acceptable) or fail to start (catastrophic). Clients must cache aggressively and degrade gracefully. **Cascade risk**: a bad config change (e.g., a timeout set to 0, a feature flag flipped prematurely) propagates to all services within seconds, taking down the system faster than a code deploy would — the same hot-reload benefit that makes dynamic config powerful also makes it dangerous. Mitigations include canary rollouts (push config to 1% of instances first), validation (schema-checked config), and audit trails (who changed what, when). **Secret management**: dynamic config servers are often misused to store secrets, but they typically lack the rotation, audit, and access-control guarantees of a dedicated secret manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager). The right split is: tunables in the config server, secrets in a secret manager, both with IAM-controlled access. **Versioning**: a config change should be versioned and reviewable like a code change — Git-backed config servers (Spring Cloud Config) make this natural; database-backed (Archaius, Diamond) make it harder and require explicit audit logging.

The deeper lesson is that configuration is a first-class artifact in a microservices system, not a side concern. It needs version control, review, audit, validation, canary rollouts, and graceful degradation — essentially the same rigor as code, because a bad config change can take down the system as thoroughly as a bad code change. The teams that get this right treat config as code (Git-backed, reviewed, tested), separate secrets from tunables (different stores, different access patterns), and invest in observability for config changes (a config-change event in the metrics, so a metric anomaly at 14:32 can be correlated with the config change at 14:31). For any microservices system above ~20 services, a config server (managed or self-hosted) is essential — the alternative is per-service env var sprawl that becomes unmaintainable within months.

sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph Sources["Configuration Sources"] ENV[Env Vars / .env file] FILE[Mounted config file] GIT[Git-backed Config Server
Spring Cloud Config] KV[Consul KV / etcd
dynamic, watch] AWS[AWS Parameter Store
+ AppConfig] VAULT[HashiCorp Vault
secrets only] end subgraph Client["Service (config layer)"] LOADER[Config Loader] CACHE[Local Cache + version] LISTENERS[Change Listeners] end subgraph Runtime["Runtime Use"] APP[Application Code] CB[Circuit Breaker threshold] FF[Feature Flag check] DB[DB connection pool] end ENV --> LOADER FILE --> LOADER GIT -->|HTTP poll / refresh| LOADER KV -->|long-poll watch| LOADER AWS -->|SDK poll| LOADER VAULT -->|TLS fetch, short-lived token| LOADER LOADER --> CACHE CACHE --> APP CACHE --> LISTENERS LISTENERS -->|hot reload| CB LISTENERS -->|hot reload| FF APP --> CB APP --> FF APP --> DB ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-------------+ +--------------+ +-----------+ | env vars |------->| | | git repo | | (secrets) | | | | (config/ | +-------------+ | | | app.yml) | | config | +-----+-----+ +-------------+ | loader | | | config.yaml |------->| (layered: |<-------------+ | (defaults) | | env > srv | +-----+-----+ +-------------+ | > file) | | consul KV | | |<-------+ (watch) | +-------------+ | | +-----------+ | vault |------->| | | (secrets) | +------+-------+ +-------------+ | v +--------------+ | local cache | version=v42 | + listeners | +------+-------+ | +--------------+--------------+ | | | v v v +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ | circuit | | feature | | rate | | breaker | | flag | | limiter | | threshold | | flag | | 1000 r/s | +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ ^ ^ ^ | hot reload on config change event | +------------------------------------+ layered precedence: base file < config server < env var static (env, file): read once at startup, restart to change dynamic (server): polled/watched, hot reload on change ``` ### Walkthrough 1. At startup, the config loader reads the base config file (defaults), overlays values from the config server (environment-specific tunables), then overlays env vars (secrets, override flags) — final value per key is the highest-precedence layer. 2. The loader caches the resolved config locally (with a version number) and registers change listeners for hot-reloadable keys (circuit-breaker thresholds, feature flags); static keys (DB URLs, secrets) are read once and require restart to change. 3. For dynamic sources (Consul KV, AWS AppConfig), the client long-polls or watches; when a value changes, the server pushes the update, the loader bumps the local version, fires change events to registered listeners, and the application reconfigures in-flight (e.g., the circuit breaker adopts the new threshold on the next call) without restart.

quiz.explanation: The config server is a runtime dependency for any service using dynamic config, and like any distributed dependency, it will fail — network partitions, server crashes, deploy-induced outages, exhausted connection pools. The service must continue operating through these failures, which means it cannot depend on the config server being reachable to serve requests.
